On such occasions poor Mr. Woodhouse found his feelings in a melancholy conflict. He liked the cloth to be laid, for it had been the fashion of his youth, yet his conviction that heavy suppers were very unwholesome made him rather uneasy at seeing anything placed upon it; and while his hospitality would have welcomed his visitors to everything, his concern for their health caused him sorrow at the thought of them eating.

A small basin of thin gruel, like his own, was all he could, with thorough self‑approval, recommend; though he might restrain himself, while the ladies were comfortably clearing away the finer dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, may I suggest you try one of these eggs? A very soft‑boiled egg is not unwholesome. Serle knows how to boil an egg better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not be frightened, they are very small, you see—one of our little eggs will not hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a _little_ bit of tart—a _very_ little bit. Ours are all apple‑tarts. You need not fear unwholesome preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Mrs. Goddard, what say you to _half_ a glass of wine? A _small_ half‑glass, diluted with water? I do not think it could disagree with you.”

Emma permitted her father to speak—but she served her guests in a far more satisfactory manner, and on that particular evening took particular pleasure in seeing them depart contented. The happiness of Miss Smith matched her intentions exactly. Miss Woodhouse was such a great figure in Highbury that the prospect of the introduction had brought both anxiety and delight; yet the modest, grateful little girl left with a highly gratified spirit, delighted by the kindness with which Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and at last even shook her hand!

I thought he might appreciate a surprise breakfast, so I slipped forward quietly and tapped his shoulder. He leapt up at once, and it was not the same figure I had seen before, but another.

Yet this second man wore the same coarse grey, bore a great iron on his leg, was lame, hoarse, shivering, and seemed to embody everything the first man had—except his face was different, and he wore a flat, broad‑brimmed, low‑crowned felt hat. I caught all this in an instant, for I had only a moment to glance: he swore at me, swung a weak, round blow that missed and almost knocked himself down, causing him to stagger, then he fled into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

“It’s the young man!” I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I might have felt a pain in my liver, too, had I known exactly where it was.

Soon after I reached the Battery, and there stood the right man—hugging himself and limping back and forth as if he had never ceased all night—waiting for me. He was terribly cold, indeed. “Brandy,” I replied.

He was already shoveling mincemeat down his throat in a most curious fashion—more like a man stuffing it away in a frantic hurry than actually eating it—but he paused to take a sip of the liquor. “You will go soon,” Miss Havisham said aloud. “Finish the game.”

Except for the odd smile at the start, I was almost certain Miss Havisham could not smile at all. Her face was fixed in a watchful, brooding look, as if everything about her had become frozen, and nothing could lift it again. She hunched her shoulders, and her voice dropped low, sounding dead and lullaby‑like; she seemed to have both body and soul pressed down by a crushing weight.

I played the game to the end with Estella, and she ruined me. She threw the cards down on the table when she had won them all, as if she despised the fact that she had taken them from me.

“When shall I have you here again?” Miss Havisham asked. “Let me think.”

I began to remind her that today was Wednesday, when she snapped at me with the impatient flick of her right hand.

“There, there! I don’t know the days of the week; I don’t know the weeks of the year. Come back in six days. Understand?”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Estella, take him down. Let him have something to eat, and let him walk around while he eats. Go, Pip.”

I followed the candle down, just as I had followed it up, and she placed it where we had found it. Until she opened the side door, I had imagined, without thinking, that it must be night. The sudden rush of daylight confused me, making me feel as if I had been in that candle‑lit room for many hours.

“You wait here, boy,” Estella said, then disappeared and closed the door.

Alone in the courtyard, I looked at my rough hands and plain boots. I didn’t like how they looked now; they seemed vulgar. I thought about asking Joe why he ever taught me to call those picture cards Jacks, when they should be called knaves. I wished Joe had been brought up more genteel, so I might have been, too.

She returned with some bread, meat, and a small mug of beer. She set the mug on the stone floor and handed me the bread and meat without looking at me, as insolently as if I were a disgraced dog.
